grammar_notes.text: The Woccon language shares the same inventory of vowels as Catawba, with twelve vowel phonemes divided into three series: four short oral vowels (i, e, a, u), four long oral vowels (i, e, a, u), and four nasal vowels (į, e, q. u).
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: The data indicate that the Woccon language shared the same inventory of vowels as the Catawba language, specifically, twelve vowel phonemes divided into three series: four short oral vowels (i, e, a, u), four long oral vowels (i, e, a, u), and four nasal vowels (į, e, q. u).

grammar_notes.text: In some words, Woccon shows a long oral vowel where Catawba exhibits a nasal vowel.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: A similar difference in the distribution of long oral vowels and nasal vowels is seen in many correspondence sets between Catawba and Woccon. In most cases, it is Woccon that shows a long oral vowel where Catawba shows a nasal vowel.

grammar_notes.text: The consonantal phonemes of Woccon include p, t, k, č, s, h, m, n, r, w, y; b and d are not attested in the data.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Based on the available evidence, the consonantal phonemes of Woccon were p, t, k, (2), č, s, h, m, n, r, w, y; there is no evidence in Lawson's vocabulary for assuming the phonemes b, d

grammar_notes.text: The phoneme s can derive from an underlying |sy| cluster or be an archaic retention from Proto-Siouan-Catawban.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: As for the phoneme s. in some cases it derives from an underlying |sy| cluster; in others it appears to be an archaic retention from Proto-Siouan-Catawban (Siebert, 1941-52)

grammar_notes.text: The distribution of m and n is different between Catawba and Woccon. In Catawba, many instances of m and n became b and d before oral vowels; this change did not occur in Woccon.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: As noted earlier, many instances of m and n became b and d, respectively, in Catawba before oral vowels, a change that did not occur in Woccon

grammar_notes.text: Short oral vowels are illustrated by forms such as *wátupi, *kus, *atusi, and *yéhiya.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Examples illustrating the short oral vowels are: *wátupi 'bottle' (W (Wattape) 'A Gourd or Bottle'; Cwátapi 'bottle'), *kus 'corn' (W (Cose) 'Corn; C kus 'corn'), *atusi 'smoke (W (Too-she) 'Smoak [sic]': Catusí soot), *yéhiya 'water' (W (Ejau) 'Water': Cyéhiye 'wa- ter')

grammar_notes.text: Long vowel phonemes are illustrated by forms such as *ku-wate, *kuware, and *rusami.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Words illustrating Woccon long vowel phonemes include: *ku-wate 'come along!' (W (Quauke) [error for Quaute] 'Will you go along with me?'; C kuwade 'come along!'), *kuware 'he kills it' (W (Caure) 'Dead', C kuwäre he kills it'), *rusami 'soft' (W (Roosomme) 'Soft', C du- 'by hand' plus samf 'fine, finely formed or made')

grammar_notes.text: Nasal vowels are illustrated by forms such as *įtu and *nimé? warápha:?.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Examples illustrating the nasal vowels are: *įtu 'pipe' (W (Intorn) 'A Tobacco-pipe'; C tu 'clay'), *nimé? warápha:? 'swine' (W (Nommewarraupau) 'Swine', Crime? 'bear' plus W (Waraupau) 'White')

grammar_notes.text: There are cases where a Woccon word has a nasal vowel and the corresponding Catawba word has a long oral vowel, as illustrated by *á ha? and *ipa.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: There are also a few cases in which a Woccon word has a nasal vowel where the corresponding Catawba word has a long oral vowel. Examples include: *á ha? 'goose' (W (Auhaun) 'A Goose'; Cá ha ? 'goose'), *ipa 'tobacco' (W (Uu-coone) [error for (Un-poone)] 'Tobac- co: Cipa 'tobacco')

grammar_notes.text: Woccon words can be simple, composed of a single morpheme (e.g., *kus 'corn', *wita? 'rat') or complex, composed of two or more morphemes (e.g., *yehu 'wind' from ye 'air' and hu 'come').
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: As in Catawba, Woccon words could be simple, .e. composed of a single morpheme (e.g., *kus 'corn' [W (Cose) 'Com': C kus 'corn'], *wita? 'rat' [W (Wittau) ‘A Rat' · C witą? 'rat']) or complex. 1.e. com- posed of two or more morphemes (e.g., *yehu 'wind' (W (Yun-cor) (error for (Yuh-hor))] 'Wind': C yehu 'wind is blowing' [from ye 'air' and hu 'come']).

grammar_notes.text: In Woccon, there is little phonological fusion of adjacent morphemes, making the morphemic composition of words nearly always transparent.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: As in Catawba, there is little phonological fusion of adjacent morphemes, and as a result, the morphemic composition of words is nearly always transparent.

grammar_notes.text: Woccon compounds follow an order where the head noun precedes the modifier (e.g., *fti tirú 'boulder', *ruisap píswa? 'stockings').
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Both Woccon and Catawba also exhibit lexemes composed of two or more words, e.g., *fti tirú 'boulder (W (Itte teraugh) 'Hard or heavy', Citi tirú 'big stone, boulder'), *ruisap píswa? 'stockings' (W (Rooesoo possoo) 'Stockings': C ísap 'leggings, trousers' plus pis 'skin' with the third person possessive suffix |-wa?).

grammar_notes.text: Reduplication is used in Woccon to signal frequency or intensity, similar to Catawba. It involves repeating the entire root.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: A fairly common feature of Catawba derivational morphology is the use of reduplication to signal frequency or intensity. It is used both with verb roots and noun roots, and takes the form of repeating the entire root.

grammar_notes.text: The initial element (Roo) or (Ru) in Woccon words may be cognate with the Catawba pronominal stem ru-. This element marks manufactured items.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Many of the words that refer to manufactured items in Lawson's list begin with an element spelled (Roo) or (Ru). In most cases the part of the word that follows this initial element can be identified with a Catawba cognate lacking the initial element.

grammar_notes.text: The independent or indicative mode in Woccon is marked by the suffix -re', which can be added to verbs, nouns, adverbs, adjectives, and particles. Examples include ká·nire• 'he/she/it sees (it)', yire 'he/she is a person', hire 'it is the one'.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: By far the most frequent mode in Catawba is the independent or indicative mode. This morpheme, which has the form -re'], may be added to verbs, nouns, adverbs, adjectives, and particles to form a predicate.

grammar_notes.text: The participial mode in Woccon is marked by the suffix --(a)?). It can occur as an ending on one of several verbs in a compound verbal construction or as a nominalizer. Examples include *iktą? 'bread', *wárapha? 'one's fever'.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Another frequent modal marker in Catawba is the participial, which has the form --(a)?). It is used both as an ending on one of the several verbs in a compound verbal construction and as a nominalizer.

grammar_notes.text: The imperative mode in Woccon appears in two constructions. In *ni kuráte ‘give me something to eat’, the form suggests that the voiced consonant of the Catawba imperative marker |-de- results from intervocalic voicing, a process attested elsewhere in the Catawba language.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: In *ni kuráte ‘give me something to eat (W (Noccoo Eraute) 'Have you got anything to cat' Cmi ku-7-ra-de- 'first singular object + give-participial-eat-impera-tive')

grammar_notes.text: The second imperative construction in Woccon is *kú·wate· ́come along!". The form suggests a possible copyist error where (t) was read as (k).
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: In the second example (1.e. *kú·wate· ́come along!" [W (Quauke) {error for (Quaute)} 'Will you go along with me?' · C kú-wade 'come along!'])

grammar_notes.text: The interrogative mode in Woccon is attested in one word: *katé-ne ‘is that all?’. The form -ne is similar to the Catawba form for interrogatives.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: The fourth mode, the interrogative, which has the form -ne in Catawba, is attested in one word: *katé-ne is that all?' (W (Cuttaune) 'That's all': C katé indeed, good-bye', katé se 'the last')

grammar_notes.text: In Woccon, the possessor of an alienably possessed noun is marked by a suffix. This pattern is similar to Catawba where inalienable possession uses prefixes and alienable possession uses suffixes.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: The same pattern of marking possessor apparently prevailed in Woccon. While there are no clear examples of inalienably possessed nouns in the Woccon data, the three examples of alienably possessed nouns mark the possessor with a suffix.

grammar_notes.text: Third person singular subjects are unmarked in Woccon.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: A couple of forms, however, indicate that third per- son singular subjects were unmarked in Woccon, e.g. *kuwá·re' (W (Caure) 'Dead' · C kuwa·re' 'he kills it'

grammar_notes.text: The creation of voiced obstruent phonemes b and d from the denasalization of m and n, regressive assimilation of voicing in consonant clusters, and the subsequent introduction of onomatopoeic vocabulary containing the sounds b and d are late developments in Catawba. This is supported by internal reconstruction within Catawba and comparison between its major dialects (Esaw and Saraw). Woccon data confirm these changes were late developments.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: Internal reconstruction within Catawba and comparison of data from the two major dialects (Esaw and Saraw) suggest that the following changes were relatively late developments in Catawba: (1) the creation of voiced obstruent phonemes b and d from the denasalization of m and n, regressive assimilation of voicing in consonant clusters, and the subsequent introduction of onomatopoeic vocabulary containing the sounds b and d;

grammar_notes.text: The elimination of r from word-initial position through nasali- zation to ʼn before nasal vowels and obstuentization to d before oral vowels is a late development in Catawba. This change is supported by internal reconstruction within Catawba and comparison between its major dialects (Esaw and Saraw). Woccon data confirm these changes were late developments.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: ... the elimination of r from word-initial position through nasali- zation to ʼn before nasal vowels and the obstuentization to d before oral vowels;

grammar_notes.text: The weakening of vowels in unstressed syllables, leading to syncope of unstressed short vowels is a late development in Catawba. This change is supported by internal reconstruction within Catawba and comparison between its major dialects (Esaw and Saraw). Woccon data confirm these changes were late developments.
grammar_notes.source_excerpt: ... the weakening of vowels in unstressed syllables, leading to syncope of unstressed short vowels (Rudes, forthcoming).

cultural_notes.text: The phoneme r is defective in Catawba and cannot occur word-initially; it appears as d before an oral vowel and n before a nasal vowel.
cultural_notes.source_excerpt: The phonemer is defective in Catawba, since it cannot occur in word-initial position. In modern Catawba, initial r appears as d before an oral vowel and n before a nasal vowel.

cultural_notes.text: The Woccon word *įtu 'pipe' refers to a tobacco pipe.

cultural_notes.text: The differences between Catawba and Woccon are not great despite their geographical distance, suggesting that other Catawban languages spoken in the Carolinas were quite similar.
